newsitem.title: USA: U.S. death toll rises as Hurricane Fran downgraded.
newsitem.headline: U.S. death toll rises as Hurricane Fran downgraded.

text.p: North and South Carolina residents wearily faced the wreckage left by Hurricane Fran on Friday as the giant storm, which left at least 12 dead, weakened and moved inland.

The damage prompted President Bill Clinton to declare North Carolina a major disaster area. "We are going to do everything we can to help the people of North Carolina," he said in a speech in Orlando, Florida.

Some 4.5 million people in the Carolinas and Virginia were left without power after Fran stormed onshore near Wilmington on Thursday night, snapping power lines, tossing signs and billboards like confetti and hurling trees into houses.

The damage was worst in northeastern North Carolina near this resort city of 60,000, where residents awoke on Friday to see fallen trees, scattered boats, signs and other debris, and some collapsed buildings. Nearby barrier islands were covered with water or isolated when ferries and roadways that link them to land were cut off by high seas and wind-blown sand.

"It's the worst storm in North Carolina since Hazel in 1954. It's so wide and so humongous," said Ben Taylor, spokesman for the North Carolina Emergency Operations Centre in Raleigh. Hazel left 95 people dead in the Carolinas.

"We're looking at some major structural damage. Roads are simply impassable, and there's nowhere for people to go," said Glen Ivey, a councilman from Kure Beach, one of three seaside communities believed to be hardest hit.

Fran was downgraded to a tropical storm before dawn on Friday, about 10 hours after its centre landed near Wilmington, spreading fierce winds, pounding waves and heavy rains over hundreds of miles (kilometers).
Fran played a hand in the presidential election campaign as well, forcing Republican nominee Bob Dole to cancel a flight to New Jersey for a speech, a campaign spokesman said.

Officials estimated on Friday morning that 95 percent of the power in the three-county area around Wilmington was out. In some areas, as much as 15 inches (37.5 cm) of rain fell and forecasters warned that flooding in areas already soaked this summer could be the storm's most serious impact. There was also a possibility of isolated tornadoes, forecasters said.

The National Hurricane Centre in Miami said that at 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT) Fran had winds of 40 mph (64 kph) and continued to weaken as it moved inland, dropping 6 to 8 inches (15-20 cms) of rain. Its centre was near Lynchburg, in central Virginia, moving north-northwest near 16 mph (26 kmh).

North Carolina officials said they had had reports of 10 deaths linked to the storm, mostly from traffic accidents and fallen trees. One of the dead was a 10-year-old boy who was killed when a tree crushed his trailer home.
South Carolina, where officials said they felt they had dodged Fran's bullet, reported two other deaths, but that seemed likely to rise after a fire in a trailer home.
